topics.title: A funny story: the giant laddoo

learn.hook: Imagine a laddoo as big as a football! Could you eat it all by yourself?
points: The lesson 'The Big Laddoo' is a funny story about a very big laddoo.
Funny stories often make things much bigger than they really are. This is called exaggeration.
'This laddoo is heavier than me!' is not really true. It is said to make us laugh.
A story also teaches us something, like the joy of sharing.

example.q:
Read:
Gopal's uncle made a giant laddoo for the school fair. It was as big as a football! Gopal tried to lift it. 'Oof!' he puffed. 'This laddoo is heavier than me!' Everyone laughed. His uncle smiled and said, 'A laddoo this big is meant for sharing.' So Gopal carried it to school in a big tin box and shared it with his whole class.
What did Gopal do with the laddoo in the end?
steps: Look at the last sentence of the story.
It says he carried it to school in a tin box.
Then he shared it with his whole class.
example.answer: He took it to school and shared it with his whole class.

learn.reallife: At a birthday party, the cake is cut into many pieces so that everyone can enjoy it, just like Gopal's laddoo.

games.title: Story order
games.prompt: Put the laddoo story in order
items: Uncle made a giant laddoo.
Gopal tried to lift it.
Gopal said it was heavier than him.
Uncle said it was meant for sharing.
Gopal shared it with his class.

games.title: True or false? (about the laddoo story)
items: The laddoo was as big as a football.
The story says 'It was as big as a football!'
Gopal ate the whole laddoo by himself.
He shared it with his whole class.
Gopal's uncle made the laddoo.
The story begins 'Gopal's uncle made a giant laddoo.'
Gopal carried the laddoo in a paper bag.
He carried it in a big tin box.
Everyone laughed at what Gopal said.
The story says 'Everyone laughed.'

quiz.q: The story begins: 'Gopal's uncle made a giant laddoo for the school fair.' Who made the laddoo?
quiz.explain: The first sentence tells us Gopal's uncle made it.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up who made the laddoo with who carried it

quiz.q: The story says: 'It was as big as a football!' How big was the laddoo?
quiz.explain: The story compares the laddoo to a football.
quiz.mistake: Did not read the comparison in the story

quiz.q: 'Gopal tried to lift it. Oof! he puffed.' Why did Gopal say 'Oof!'?
options: because the laddoo was very heavy
quiz.explain: People say 'Oof!' when lifting something heavy.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect 'Oof!' with lifting a heavy thing

quiz.q: Gopal says, 'This laddoo is heavier than me!' Why is this line funny?
options: A laddoo cannot really be heavier than a boy.
quiz.explain: It is an exaggeration, said to make us laugh.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the line is meant to be true

quiz.q: Uncle says, 'A laddoo this big is meant for sharing.' What does he mean?
options: The laddoo should be thrown away.
A big laddoo should be shared with others.
quiz.explain: He means it is too big for one person and should be shared.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand what 'meant for sharing' means

quiz.q: The story says Gopal 'carried it to school in a big tin box'. How did Gopal carry the laddoo?
quiz.explain: The story says he used a big tin box.
quiz.mistake: Guessed instead of reading the line

quiz.q: The story ends: 'shared it with his whole class.' Who did Gopal share the laddoo with?
quiz.explain: He shared it with his whole class.
quiz.mistake: Did not read the last sentence

quiz.q: The story calls it 'a giant laddoo'. What does 'giant' mean?
quiz.explain: 'Giant' means very, very big.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'giant'

teach.ask: Gappu giggles and asks: 'Why is the big laddoo story funny? What did Gopal do with it?'
teach.praise: Ha ha! A laddoo heavier than a boy! And he shared it with everyone. Yum!
teach.nudge: Can you tell me why the story is funny and what Gopal did with the laddoo?

learn.hook: Your friend forgot her tiffin. You have four parathas. What will you do?
points: Sharing means giving a part of what you have to others.
Wash your hands with soap before you eat or share food.
Ask your friend before you offer food. Some children cannot eat some foods.
Share fairly, so everyone gets an equal part.
Take only as much as you can eat, so no food is wasted.

example.q: Riya has 6 biscuits. She shares them equally with her friend Aman. How many does each get?
steps: Equally means both get the same number.
So Riya gets 3 and Aman gets 3.

learn.reallife: In the school lunch break, at a wedding feast or at a family picnic, people share food and eat together.

games.title: Good sharing habit or not?
items: washing hands before eating
asking a friend before offering food
saying thank you
sharing fairly
snatching food from a friend
taking food and throwing half away
eating a friend's tiffin without asking
laughing at a friend's food

items.text: When a friend shares food with me, I say ___.
Before eating, we should ___ our hands.
A person who happily shares is ___.

quiz.q: Which is a good sharing habit?
options: offering food to a friend who has none
eating a friend's tiffin without asking
quiz.explain: Offering food to a friend who has none is kind sharing.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that taking without asking is unkind

quiz.q: What should you do before eating?
quiz.explain: Washing hands with soap removes germs before we eat.
quiz.mistake: Forgets about clean hands

quiz.q: Riya has 6 biscuits. She shares them equally with one friend. How many biscuits does each child get?
quiz.explain: 6 shared equally between 2 children is 3 each.
quiz.mistake: Does not divide equally between the two children

quiz.q: Before you offer your food to a friend, what is a good thing to do?
options: ask if they would like some
quiz.explain: Asking first is polite. Some children cannot eat some foods.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you should give food without asking

quiz.q: What does 'share' mean?
options: to give a part of what you have to others
quiz.explain: Sharing means giving a part of what we have to others.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sharing with keeping

quiz.q: A friend shares her poha with you. What should you say?
quiz.explain: We say 'thank you' when someone shares with us.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to be polite

quiz.q: Which of these is wasting food?
options: taking more than you can eat and throwing it away
eating what is on your plate
keeping leftovers safely in the fridge
quiz.explain: Throwing away good food is wasting it.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that taking too much leads to waste

quiz.q: Someone who does not like to share at all is called ___.
quiz.explain: A selfish person keeps everything for themselves.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the words selfish and generous

teach.ask: Gappu has a big bunch of grapes. He asks: 'How should I share them with my friends?'
teach.praise: I will wash my wings, ask my friends and share the grapes equally!
teach.nudge: Can you tell me how to share food in a fair and polite way?

learn.hook: A laddoo is big. A football is bigger. An elephant is the biggest! Let's compare!
points: We add -er to compare two things: 'This laddoo is bigger than that one.'
We add -est to compare three or more things: 'Gopal's laddoo is the biggest of all.'
Some words double the last letter: big – bigger – biggest, hot – hotter – hottest.
Words ending in y change y to i: happy – happier – happiest.
Some words change fully: good – better – best.

example.q: Fill in: 'Gopal's laddoo is ___ than Raju's laddoo.' (big)
example.answer: Gopal's laddoo is bigger than Raju's laddoo.

learn.reallife: When you compare heights in class, you say 'Raju is taller than me', and 'Meena is the tallest'.

games.title: Smallest to biggest
games.prompt: Put these in order from smallest to biggest
items: a mustard seed
a pea
a laddoo
a football
an elephant

games.title: Match the word to its -est form

quiz.q: Fill in: 'This laddoo is ___ than that one.'
quiz.explain: We compare two laddoos, so we use 'bigger'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the -est form when comparing only two things

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Gopal's laddoo was the ___ of all the laddoos at the fair.'
quiz.explain: We compare many laddoos, so we use 'biggest'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the -er form when comparing many things

quiz.q: How do we spell big + er?
quiz.explain: 'big' doubles the 'g' before -er: bigger.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the last letter

quiz.q: good, better, ___
quiz.explain: good – better – best. These words change fully.
quiz.mistake: Adds -est to 'good'

quiz.q: small, smaller, ___
quiz.explain: small – smaller – smallest.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the -est form

quiz.q: Fill in: 'A jalebi is ___ than a lemon.' (sweet)
quiz.explain: Two things are compared, so we use 'sweeter'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the -est form when comparing two things

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Meena was ___ than her brother when she won the prize.' (happy)
quiz.explain: We change y to i and add -er: happier.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change y to i

quiz.q: Which word compares three or more things?
quiz.explain: '-est' words like 'hottest' compare three or more things.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the -er and -est forms

teach.ask: Gappu sees three laddoos. He asks: 'When do I say bigger and when do I say biggest?'
teach.praise: This laddoo is bigger than that one, and that one is the biggest of all! I get it!
teach.nudge: Can you tell me when we use '-er' and when we use '-est'?
